Biofuel - an opportunity lost?

By: Hein Kaiser | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we investigate whether biofuel can solve our energy deficit while creating jobs and reducing emissions. But not everyone agrees and government seems indecisive.

Unique Selling Point:
Environmental and emission reductions, the dependency on fossil fuels and unemployment are all significant challenges facing South Africa. A robust biofuel industry may contribute to solving these challenges in part. But not everyone thinks so, and government seems to be indecisive. Carte Blacnhe investigates.

Summary:
Biofuel can be a solution to two major problems and create new opportunity for South Africa.
Biofuel can possibly reduce dependency on fossil fuels and, by doing so, also reduce emissions as a result of fossil fuels. It can also create thousands of new jobs, save on forex payments and earn forex for South Africa.
But nothing is happening. And environmentalists say its not the panacea that its proponents make it out to be.


Further information:
Biofuel can be a solution to two major problems and create new opportunity for South Africa.
Biofuel can possibly reduce dependency on fossil fuels and, by doing so, also reduce emissions as a result of fossil fuels. It can also create thousands of new jobs, save on forex payments and earn forex for South Africa.
But nothing is happening. And environmentalists say its not the panacea that its proponents make it out to be.
Dr Ian Cruickshank is a pioneer in biofuels. He developed SAA’s biofuel programme and headed the project to fly 2 aircraft to Cape Town on locally grown biofuel (from Solaris). He is passionate about its potential.
We go back to this project and bring it to today, where the global energy crisis and growing action around climate change is accelerating the call for more biofuel to be produced and blended with Diesel for cars and trucks while, for airlines, to power flights entirely. Dr Cruickshank heads up IATA’s task team for this and heads up the Transportation Division of Prince William’s Wildlife Trust.
But organisations like Greenpeace says that biofuel holds several environmental hazards, and that gains on the one side come with massive opportunity costs like threats to food security on the one hand and say that burning down forests for cultivation of biofuel feedstock on the other creates even greater environmental damage. We explore this with Greenpeace and get to know a little more, in the process, about the organisation and the dymanics that inform its position, and the people who contemplate it.
Yet, Craig Williamson of Green Diesel says that feedstock is not the only source of biofuel. He has been making it for years, albeit his factory now stands still because millions of litres of cooking oil is being exported to the EU. He still builds small refineries for companies. Craig shared that used cooking oil, animal and other organic waste can also produce biofuel. A client of his makes his own biofuel to part power his fleet of trucks….. (Benoni blended Diesel plant)
In fact, with changing legislation government will expect a 50% reduction in organic waste on landfills. And Craig says that a significant portion of this kind of waste can be recycled into energy.
Craig has also built a mobile biofuel unit for an NGO in Limpopo that trains young aspiring entrepreneurs how to make the fuel. But, because regulations limits the sale of it, it is limited to 300 000 litres annually. they cannot make a living.
And biofuel holds a lot of economic potential. The WWF said in a report that it can create thousands of jobs, and for every 1 litre of biofuel combusted, it saves 7 kg of greenhouse gas.
We visit the Limpopo project, and we drive there on a tank of blended biofuel.
Yet there is no enforcement of the current legislation where 2% biofuel must be blended with Diesel. And, we cannot make any, because the cooking oil is being exported. There’s also a working group in DME, that doesn’t do much. We have no real framework to develop in industry that holds significant potential for our economy, and for the environment.
But Greenpeace says this is not so, and the damage large scale biofuel production will cause is significant.
Dr Cruickshank says that biofuel can be properly certified and echoes the economic potential. He also says that the mothballed refineries can be repurposed and that tobacco farms on existing farmland can be used to harvest biofuel feedstock.
So where does this leave biofuel? Did South Africa miss a huge opportunity? Or are we dodging an environmental bullet by doing nothing?
And why do we have no real framework to take it forward, or to scrap it? There’s only a 2007 Biofuel Industrialisation paper that is dated and not enforced. We ask DME, too.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we investigate whether biofuel can solve our energy deficit while creating jobs and reducing emissions. But not everyone agrees and government seems indecisive.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Environmental and emission reductions, the dependency on fossil fuels and unemployment are all significant challenges facing South Africa. A robust biofuel industry may contribute to solving these challenges in part. But not everyone thinks so, and government seems to be indecisive. Carte Blacnhe investigates.
metadata.Summary: Biofuel can be a solution to two major problems and create new opportunity for South Africa. Biofuel can possibly reduce dependency on fossil fuels and, by doing so, also reduce emissions as a result of fossil fuels. It can also create thousands of new jobs, save on forex payments and earn forex for South Africa. But nothing is happening. And environmentalists say its not the panacea that its proponents make it out to be.
metadata.Further information: Biofuel can be a solution to two major problems and create new opportunity for South Africa. Biofuel can possibly reduce dependency on fossil fuels and, by doing so, also reduce emissions as a result of fossil fuels. It can also create thousands of new jobs, save on forex payments and earn forex for South Africa. But nothing is happening. And environmentalists say its not the panacea that its proponents make it out to be. Dr Ian Cruickshank is a pioneer in biofuels. He developed SAA’s biofuel programme and headed the project to fly 2 aircraft to Cape Town on locally grown biofuel (from Solaris). He is passionate about its potential. We go back to this project and bring it to today, where the global energy crisis and growing action around climate change is accelerating the call for more biofuel to be produced and blended with Diesel for cars and trucks while, for airlines, to power flights entirely. Dr Cruickshank heads up IATA’s task team for this and heads up the Transportation Division of Prince William’s Wildlife Trust. But organisations like Greenpeace says that biofuel holds several environmental hazards, and that gains on the one side come with massive opportunity costs like threats to food security on the one hand and say that burning down forests for cultivation of biofuel feedstock on the other creates even greater environmental damage. We explore this with Greenpeace and get to know a little more, in the process, about the organisation and the dymanics that inform its position, and the people who contemplate it. Yet, Craig Williamson of Green Diesel says that feedstock is not the only source of biofuel. He has been making it for years, albeit his factory now stands still because millions of litres of cooking oil is being exported to the EU. He still builds small refineries for companies. Craig shared that used cooking oil, animal and other organic waste can also produce biofuel. A client of his makes his own biofuel to part power his fleet of trucks….. (Benoni blended Diesel plant) In fact, with changing legislation government will expect a 50% reduction in organic waste on landfills. And Craig says that a significant portion of this kind of waste can be recycled into energy. Craig has also built a mobile biofuel unit for an NGO in Limpopo that trains young aspiring entrepreneurs how to make the fuel. But, because regulations limits the sale of it, it is limited to 300 000 litres annually. they cannot make a living. And biofuel holds a lot of economic potential. The WWF said in a report that it can create thousands of jobs, and for every 1 litre of biofuel combusted, it saves 7 kg of greenhouse gas. We visit the Limpopo project, and we drive there on a tank of blended biofuel. Yet there is no enforcement of the current legislation where 2% biofuel must be blended with Diesel. And, we cannot make any, because the cooking oil is being exported. There’s also a working group in DME, that doesn’t do much. We have no real framework to develop in industry that holds significant potential for our economy, and for the environment. But Greenpeace says this is not so, and the damage large scale biofuel production will cause is significant. Dr Cruickshank says that biofuel can be properly certified and echoes the economic potential. He also says that the mothballed refineries can be repurposed and that tobacco farms on existing farmland can be used to harvest biofuel feedstock. So where does this leave biofuel? Did South Africa miss a huge opportunity? Or are we dodging an environmental bullet by doing nothing? And why do we have no real framework to take it forward, or to scrap it? There’s only a 2007 Biofuel Industrialisation paper that is dated and not enforced. We ask DME, too.
